summary: This document defines additional MODP Diffie-Hellman groups for SSH that use SHA-2 hashes. It also updates RFC 4250 and updates RFC 4253 by correcting an error about checking the peer's Diffie-Hellman public key.

plainLanguage.summary: SSH needs to agree on a secret with big numbers. This adds more choices of numbers and fixes a mistake in how one side checks the other's.

subtitle: Five new Diffie-Hellman key exchange methods for SSH, all with SHA-2 hashes, plus a fix to how peers' public keys are range-checked.

tldr.problem: SSH key exchange relied on SHA-1 and on MODP groups smaller than 2048 bits, which raised security concerns, and RFC 4253 also contained a small error in the range check for the peer's Diffie-Hellman public key.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five new key exchange method names that pair MODP groups 14 through 18 with SHA-256 or SHA-512, and corrects the public key check to the open interval 1 < value < p-1.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers get stronger, standardized key exchange choices, and the corrected check keeps a peer from forcing the local system into a two-element subgroup.

today: RFC 8268 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2017. It updates RFC 4250 and RFC 4253, and it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Overview and Rationale
sections.content:
RFC 8268 extends Secure Shell (SSH) with new Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange methods that use Modular Exponentiation (MODP) groups and SHA-2 hashes. It does two jobs: it adds new method names, and it corrects an error in RFC 4253.

The motivation is security concern about SHA-1 and about MODP groups with fewer than 2048 bits. The RFC asks implementers and users to request larger MODP groups and the SHA-2 family of hash algorithms. It also says the new methods are intended to update Section 6.4 of RFC 4253 and Section 4.10 of RFC 4250.

The DH primes adopted here are all safe primes, meaning p = 2q + 1 where q is also prime.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the old secret-sharing tricks in SSH are getting too easy to crack. This RFC adds stronger ones and fixes one small mistake in the rulebook.

sections.title: Why These Groups and Hashes
sections.content:
The RFC explains its choices by pointing to an FAQ from the United States Information Assurance Directorate at the National Security Agency, written for operators of national security systems. That FAQ says such systems should stop using SHA-256, AES-128, RSA with 2048-bit keys and Diffie-Hellman with 2048-bit keys, and should use a Diffie-Hellman prime modulus of at least 3072 bits.

For SSH, the RFC translates this into avoiding key exchange with SHA1, SHA224 or SHA256 in favor of SHA384 or SHA512. For DH sizes in RFC 3526, groups 15, 16, 17 and 18 meet the 3072-bit minimum.

The RFC adopts those example groups and uses SHA512 rather than SHA256 for the new groups, while admitting that SSH may not always protect Top Secret communications.
sections.plainLanguage: A big security agency said that small locks are no longer good enough. So SSH gets some much bigger locks to pick from.

sections.title: The New Key Exchange Methods
sections.content:
Five method names are defined: diffie-hellman-group14-sha256, diffie-hellman-group15-sha512, diffie-hellman-group16-sha512, diffie-hellman-group17-sha512 and diffie-hellman-group18-sha512. They follow the style and conventions of RFC 4253, and the SHA-2 hashes are defined in RFC 6234.

The group14-sha256 method works exactly like diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 except that SHA256 is the hash. It is included because the 2048-bit group14 is already in most SSH implementations, and most already have SHA256, so it is easy to implement. It SHOULD be supported to smooth the transition to newer group sizes.

The group15 through group18 names use the groups from RFC 3526: 3072-bit group15, 4096-bit group16, 6144-bit group17 and 8192-bit group18. Whenever sha512 appears in the method name, SHA512 is the hash.
sections.plainLanguage: There are now five new recipes for agreeing on a secret. Each one picks a lock size and a scrambler, and the bigger the lock number, the tougher it is.

sections.title: Checking the Peer's DH Public Key
sections.content:
Section 8 of RFC 4253 says values of e (the client's public key) or f (the server's public key) outside the range [1, p-1] must not be sent or accepted. The RFC calls this a small error: the range should have excluded both endpoints, as an open interval.

The corrected rule is that both 1 < e < p-1 and 1 < f < p-1 MUST be true. Values outside these bounds MUST NOT be sent or accepted by either side, and if either condition is violated the key exchange fails.

The RFC says this simple check ensures that the remote peer behaves properly and that the local system is not forced into the two-element subgroup.
sections.plainLanguage: When the other side hands you a number, you must check it is not one of the two silly numbers at the very edges. If it is, the whole deal is off.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added the five new method names to the "Key Exchange Method Names" registry, each with RFC 8268 as its reference. The names are the same five listed in the algorithms section above.

This is what lets SSH clients and servers announce and agree on these methods by name during negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The five new recipes were written down in an official list, so everyone uses the same names for them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4253 apply. RFC 3526 suggests that MODP group14 through group18 have security strengths ranging from 110 bits to 310 bits, based on RFC 3766. The RFC adds that care should be taken to use sufficient entropy or deterministic random-bit generator (DRBG) algorithms to maximize the true security strength of the key exchange and ciphers selected.

It also warns that a fixed set of DH parameters is a high-value target for pre-computation. Generating additional sets of primes, or moving to larger values, mitigates this issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Everybody using the same big numbers makes them a juicy target, so bigger numbers or fresh ones help keep the secret safe.
